opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one we spent a lot of time thinking about before we committed to this direction.

The core intuition is this: the sim-to-real visual gap was a really serious problem back when policies were trained from scratch, or with a small vision backbone that only ever saw synthetic images. In that setting, the network learns whatever shortcuts are available in the rendered pixels: the particular way the renderer handles shadows, the slightly-too-clean textures, the lighting. Then you put it in the real world and those cues are all different, and the policy falls apart.

A VLM changes the picture because its visual representation was not learned from our simulation at all. It was learned from billions of real-world images paired with language. So by the time we bring in our synthetic manipulation data, the model already has a very robust, very semantic understanding of what a cup is, what a drawer handle is, what "the red one on the left" means. Those concepts are anchored in real-world visual statistics.

What we're doing with the rendered data, then, is mostly teaching the action side: how to grasp, how to move, how geometry relates to motion. We're not asking the model to relearn vision from synthetic pixels. If you keep that pretrained visual-language knowledge intact, and you co-train with some real or internet data so the representation doesn't drift, the model tends to map both a rendered mug and a real mug into a very similar internal concept. The gap gets absorbed at the representation level instead of at the pixel level.

The second piece is that our rendering quality has improved a lot. With good physically based rendering, plus heavy randomization of lighting, materials, backgrounds, and camera poses, the synthetic images are no longer that far from reality. You don't need it to be perfect. You need it to be close enough, and diverse enough, that the real world looks like just another sample from the distribution. Combining large-scale, diverse synthetic data with a strong pretrained VLM is what makes zero-shot transfer actually work.

And empirically, that's what we've seen. When we train on purely synthetic action data on top of a VLM backbone, we can deploy directly in real scenes and the success rates are surprisingly strong, in cluttered environments, with novel objects, under different lighting. That convinced us the visual gap is no longer the main bottleneck. The harder problems now are more on the physics side: contact, dynamics, deformable objects. That's where the real frontier for simulation is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the visual gap and sim-to-real transfer but never compares that gap with the gap between cartoon characters and the real world.

r002.rationale: It explains that pretrained VLM representations map rendered and real objects to similar concepts, while rendered data teaches action, geometry, and motion—allowing the model to bridge visual differences at the representation level.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key is that the visual gap isn't really the robot's problem anymore. It's the vision backbone's problem, and the backbone has already solved it.

When we build a VLA on top of a large vision-language model, that model has been pre-trained on billions of internet images: real photos, cartoons, renders, game screenshots, sketches, everything. So its visual features are already quite invariant to style. A cup in a ray-traced simulator and a cup on a messy lab table map to roughly the same place in its representation space, because it has learned that "cupness" is about shape, context and semantics, not about pixel-level texture or lighting noise. The classic sim-to-real gap that killed earlier end-to-end policies was a gap in low-level appearance, and that is exactly the dimension a VLM has learned to ignore.

So when we train the action head on synthetic data, what the policy is really learning is the mapping from semantic understanding to motion. Where is the handle, which way does the drawer open, how do I approach without colliding. That knowledge is physics and geometry, and physics simulation gets that right. We are not asking the simulator to look exactly like the world. We are asking it to be correct about contact, mass, friction and kinematics, and then letting the VLM's perception absorb the appearance differences.

There's also a scale argument. Real robot data is expensive and narrow. Synthetic data lets us render the same task across thousands of textures, lighting conditions, camera poses and object instances. With a VLM in the loop, that domain randomization is no longer a trick to force invariance from scratch, it is just reinforcing an invariance the model already has. In our experiments, policies trained almost entirely on rendered data transfer to real scenes with very little or no real fine-tuning, and when we do mix in a small amount of real data, it is mostly to calibrate the action distribution, not to fix perception.

I'd be careful about one thing, though. The VLM closes the gap at the level of what is seen, not at the level of how things behave. If your simulator gets deformables wrong, or contact dynamics wrong, no amount of visual generalization will save you. So the honest framing is: VLM handles the appearance gap, and physics fidelity has to handle the dynamics gap. Both matter, but the appearance side used to be the bottleneck, and I think it largely isn't anymore.

r001.rationale: The response mentions cartoons among the VLM’s pretraining images but does not compare the cartoon-to-real-world gap with the rendered-manipulation-to-real-world gap.

r002.rationale: It says the VLM’s visual features are invariant to style and that the action head learns the mapping from semantic understanding—such as locating a handle and determining how a drawer opens—to motion despite appearance differences.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that a VLM-based VLA doesn’t have to learn visual understanding from scratch using only rendered robot data. The vision-language model has already been pretrained on a broad range of real-world images, so it brings representations of objects, materials, and scenes that are much richer than what we could learn from a relatively narrow manipulation dataset.

Then the simulated robot data teaches it how those visual concepts connect to actions—where to move, how to grasp, and what happens after contact. The hope is that an object in simulation and its real-world counterpart activate sufficiently similar representations that the learned behavior transfers, even when their pixels look different.

But I wouldn’t say that pretraining automatically eliminates the visual gap. Manipulation requires precise spatial information, and recognizing a cup is different from locating its rim accurately enough to grasp it. So rendering quality, visual diversity, and preserving the pretrained representations during action training still matter. The VLM gives us a strong bridge across that gap; simulation supplies the action experience.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the visual gap with physically rendered manipulation data to the gap between cartoon characters and the real world.

r002.rationale: It says simulated data teaches how visual concepts connect to manipulation actions and that behavior can transfer when simulated and real-world pixels differ.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that a VLM brings a visual representation that has already learned from a broad range of real-world images. So when we build a VLA on top of it, we’re not asking it to learn what the world looks like purely from rendered robot data. We’re mainly asking it to learn how visual observations and language instructions map to actions.

For example, a rendered cup and a real cup may differ in texture, lighting, or background, but the pretrained VLM may still recognize both as a cup and capture features relevant to grasping it. That gives the policy a starting point that is less dependent on the exact appearance of the simulator.

But I wouldn’t say this automatically eliminates the visual gap. Manipulation requires precise spatial information, and recognizing an object is different from knowing exactly where to place the gripper. The potential comes from combining that broad visual knowledge with physically grounded action training, while preserving the useful representations during training.
